Likely attempts and what to say: (1) 'about 50 m' or '40 m', a number copied from the problem: ask 'Is an angle in degrees the same kind of number as a length in metres?'; (2) 40 + 50 or 40 × 50, mixing the angle and the distance: ask 'What unit does each number have?'; (3) a correct diagram but 'stuck': praise the diagram as the right first step and say the missing piece is the link between the angle and the sides; (4) a sensible estimate from a scale sketch (for example 45 to 50 m): accept it as an estimate to be checked in Lesson 2, and do not reveal the value (about 47.7 m).

records.why: Lesson 2 is a 40-minute single period. The activities as written added up to about 47 minutes (two new triangles drawn and measured, six ratio sets computed, class table, table look-up, definitions, mast example, two practice problems, board update, model). Learners already measured 40° triangles in Lesson 1, so they reuse them and only switch to the other acute angle (50°). This removes about 8 minutes, keeps the key idea (labels swap when the reference angle changes) and gives the 40°/50° pair that Lesson 3 needs. The same idea (50° is the mast angle) strengthens the link to the phenomenon.
records.old: In pairs, learners draw two fresh right-angled triangles in their exercise books — one with an estimated acute angle of about 35° and one with about 60° — using ruler and protractor. They measure all three sides to the nearest millimetre. For each triangle, they choose each acute angle in turn as the reference angle, label O, A, H correctly, and compute all three ratios (O/H, A/H, O/A) to 3 decimal places. They record all six sets of ratios in a personal table.
records.new: In pairs, learners take the three 40° triangles they drew and measured in Lesson 1 (no new drawing). They choose one triangle, label O, A, H from the 40° angle, and then switch to the other acute angle (50°), re-label O, A, H, and compute all three ratios (O/H, A/H, O/A) to 3 decimal places for each angle. They record the six ratios in a personal table (angle, sin, cos, tan).

records.old: Distribute rulers and protractors. Say: 'Draw two right-angled triangles — make them different sizes. Estimate one angle at about 35° and in the other about 60°. Measure all three sides. Then, for EACH acute angle in EACH triangle, label which side is opposite, which is adjacent, which is hypotenuse — remember, these labels CHANGE when you switch which angle you look from. Compute O÷H, A÷H, O÷A. Record everything.' [Circulate for 8 minutes. At each pair, ask: 'You have switched to the other acute angle — have your labels changed? Show me.'] After 8 minutes, draw the class table on the board. Point to pairs one by one: 'Otieno and Kamau — give me your sin of 35°.' Fill in the table. records.old:
The Observe Phase is the lesson's practical core. In pairs, learners draw two different right-angled triangles (angles of their choice between 20° and 70°), measure sides, compute the three ratios for both acute angles in each triangle, and record results in a shared class table on the board. They immediately notice that switching the reference angle swaps the "opposite" and "adjacent" labels — a crucial insight for avoiding the most common labelling error. Learners then open mathematical tables (sine, cosine, tangent pages) and locate the values for their measured angles, comparing table values to their computed ratios and experiencing the power of the table as a pre-computed library of ratios.

In the Explain Phase

records.why: The old check said sin and cos of the same angle should 'roughly sum near 1'. That is false: sin 35° + cos 35° = 0.574 + 0.819 = 1.39, sin 60° + cos 60° = 0.866 + 0.500 = 1.37, and at 45° the sum is 1.41. It is the SQUARES that add to 1 (sin² + cos² = 1). A teacher following the old note would have 'corrected' correct tables. Rechecked with table values: sin 40° = 0.6428, cos 40° = 0.7660, sin 50° = 0.7660, cos 50° = 0.6428, so sin 40° + cos 40° = 1.4088.
records.old: Look at the class table on the board: if the sin and cos columns for the same angle do not roughly sum near 1 (not exactly — that is Lesson 3), a labelling or calculation error likely exists. Identify and address publicly.
records.new: Look at the class table on the board. Sin and cos of an acute angle are always less than 1 (the hypotenuse is the longest side), and their sum is NOT 1 (for example sin 40° + cos 40° ≈ 0.643 + 0.766 = 1.41), so any sin or cos value of 1 or more is an error. Also check that sin 40° and cos 50° are nearly equal, and so are sin 50° and cos 40°; if they are not, a pair has mixed up opposite and adjacent (the reason is Lesson 3). Identify and address errors publicly.
records.reference: Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1: OpenStax, Algebra and Trigonometry, chapter on right-triangle trigonometry and trigonometric identities; KICD Grade 10 Mathematics, 2.4 Trigonometry 1
records.group_headline: Lesson 2 claimed sin and cos of one angle add to about 1 (false: sin 35° + cos 35° is about 1.39; it is the squares that add to 1); replaced with a correct error check

records.why: 'For the same angle, as sin goes up, cos goes down' is not meaningful (one angle has one sin and one cos). The true pattern is across angles: as the angle grows, sin increases and cos decreases. Checked with tables: sin 40° = 0.643 < sin 50° = 0.766; cos 40° = 0.766 > cos 50° = 0.643.

records.new: Notice that as the angle gets bigger, sin goes up and cos goes down, and sin 40° looks the same as cos 50° — we will explore why in Lesson 3. For now, simply observe it in the table.

records.old: The lesson opens by returning — at last — to the very image that launched the unit eight lessons ago: the Kenya Power electricity transmission tower standing near a school in Nakuru County. A student 40 m from the base measured the elevation angle as approximately 50°. In every previous lesson learners have been building the tools needed to answer the question the phenomenon posed: how tall is that mast? Now, in the Predict Phase, learners revisit their Lesson 1 guesses and write down their best calculation before any class discussion. In the Observe Phase they watch or reconstruct the step-by-step solution as a worked example, verifying their own working and encountering the answer — approximately 47.7 m — for the first time with full mathematical confidence.

records.why: The summative task could not work. It said the boat sees the lighthouse top at 38° elevation and the lighthouse top sees the same boat at 22° depression. Those are the same line of sight, so the two angles must be equal (alternate angles), and the mark scheme in the teacher moves broke down in front of the class (it even asked students to find a negative height). The same story also appeared with different numbers (32° and 25°) in the overview. Fix: the 22° depression is now measured by an observer at the TOP OF THE CLIFF, so it equals the elevation of the cliff top from the boat, and 38° is measured to the lighthouse top. Checked twice: cliff = 120 x tan 22° = 120 x 0.40403 = 48.48 m; lighthouse top = 120 x tan 38° = 120 x 0.78129 = 93.75 m; lighthouse = 93.75 - 48.48 = 45.27 m (45.3 m from the rounded values 93.8 - 48.5). Teacher must decide whether to keep a lighthouse setting (the Kisumu shore has few cliffs; a rocky hill with a communications mast would also work with the same numbers).
records.old: A lighthouse stands on the edge of a cliff on the shore of Lake Victoria. A fisherman in a boat 120 m from the base of the cliff observes the top of the lighthouse at an angle of elevation of 38°. A coastguard at the top of the lighthouse observes the same boat at an angle of depression of 22°. (a) Calculate the height of the lighthouse above the water. (b) Calculate the height of the cliff (to the nearest metre). (c) Hence find the total height of the lighthouse structure above the base of the cliff.'
records.new: A lighthouse stands at the top of a cliff on the shore of Lake Victoria near Kisumu. A fisherman in a boat on the water, 120 m horizontally from the foot of the cliff, measures the angle of elevation of the top of the lighthouse as 38°. A coastguard officer standing at the top of the cliff, at the foot of the lighthouse, measures the angle of depression of the same boat as 22°. (Ignore the eye heights of the observers.) (a) Calculate the height of the cliff above the water, to one decimal place. (b) Calculate the height of the top of the lighthouse above the water. (c) Hence find the height of the lighthouse itself, from the top of the cliff to its top.'
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 Mathematics, 2.4 Trigonometry 1 (angles of elevation and depression); alternate angles between parallel lines, Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 29
records.group_headline: Lighthouse assessment was geometrically impossible (38° elevation and 22° depression along one line of sight must be equal); redesigned so the depression angle is measured from the cliff top and the numbers give a consistent answer

records.why: Replaces the mark scheme that contradicted itself (it produced a negative cliff height and then called this 'intentional') with a correct worked mark scheme and look-fors for the new task. Arithmetic checked twice: tan 22° = 0.40403, tan 38° = 0.78129; 120 x 0.40403 = 48.48; 120 x 0.78129 = 93.75; difference 45.27 m.
records.old: Display the mark scheme on the board and read each step aloud: '(a) tan 38° = h₁ ÷ 120, so h₁ = 120 × tan 38° ≈ 120 × 0.7813 ≈ 93.8 m — that is the height of the lighthouse above the cliff top. (b) tan 22° = h₂ ÷ 120, so h₂ = 120 × tan 22° ≈ 120 × 0.4040 ≈ 48.5 m — that is the total height from water to lighthouse top; thus cliff height = 48.5 − 93.8 ... ' — pause and cold-call: 'Wait — does that make sense? Akinyi, what is wrong with that arithmetic?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Guide class to recognise the two triangles share the 120 m base but measure different vertical heights. Correct interpretation: (b) the angle of depression of 22° from the lighthouse top to the boat gives the total height (cliff + lighthouse) = 120 × tan 22° ≈ 48.5 m; part (c) cliff height = total − lighthouse = 48.5 − 93.8 is negative, which is impossible — prompt class to re-examine which angle corresponds to which height. Lead class to correct setup: angle of elevation 38° gives height of the full structure above water = 120 × tan 38° ≈ 93.8 m; angle of depression 22° from lighthouse top gives total height above water = 120 × tan 22° ≈ 48.5 m. Since 48.5 < 93.8, revisit the problem — the lighthouse top is higher, so the angle of depression should be larger for the closer structure. This productive contradiction is intentional: say 'This is mathematics working as it should — the numbers are telling us something. Let us re-read the problem together.' Re-examine and clarify that the angle of elevation to the lighthouse top (38°) gives total height = 93.8 m, and angle of depression from lighthouse top (22°) also gives the same total height (alternate interior angles) ≈ 48.5 m, which now reveals an inconsistency designed to promote critical thinking. Conclude: 'Real problems need careful diagram work. The diagram saves you every time.'
records.new: Display the mark scheme on the board and read each step aloud: 'Diagram 1 (boat to cliff top): the 22° angle of depression at the cliff top equals the 22° angle of elevation at the boat (alternate angles). (a) tan 22° = h₁ ÷ 120, so h₁ = 120 × tan 22° ≈ 120 × 0.4040 ≈ 48.5 m, the height of the cliff above the water. Diagram 2 (boat to lighthouse top): (b) tan 38° = h₂ ÷ 120, so h₂ = 120 × tan 38° ≈ 120 × 0.7813 ≈ 93.8 m, the height of the lighthouse top above the water. (c) Height of the lighthouse = h₂ − h₁ ≈ 93.8 − 48.5 = 45.3 m.' Look-fors and what to say: (i) a learner who uses 38° for the cliff or 22° for the lighthouse top: ask 'Which angle is measured to the cliff top and which to the lighthouse top? Mark each on your diagram.'; (ii) a learner who draws the 22° inside the triangle at the top, between the cliff and the line of sight: ask 'From which line is an angle of depression measured?'; (iii) a learner who gives 93.8 m as the lighthouse height: ask 'Is 93.8 m measured from the water or from the top of the cliff?' Sense check: the lighthouse top (93.8 m) must be higher than the cliff top (48.5 m), and it is. Conclude: 'Real problems need careful diagram work. The diagram saves you every time.'
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 Mathematics, 2.4 Trigonometry 1 (angles of elevation and depression); alternate angles between parallel lines, Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 29

records.why: Diagram B gives the vertical rise (20 m, opposite side) and asks for the horizontal distance (adjacent side). The ratio that links opposite and adjacent is tangent. Sine would give the sloping road length, not the horizontal distance, so 'accept either' was wrong. Checked: tan 35° = 0.7002, 20 / 0.7002 = 28.56 m; sin 35° = 0.5736, 20 / 0.5736 = 34.87 m.
records.old: Diagram B → sine (opposite/hypotenuse ... or tan — accept either with valid reasoning)
records.new: Diagram B → tangent (opposite and adjacent: horizontal distance = 20 ÷ tan 35° ≈ 28.6 m). A learner who chooses sine is finding the length of the road (20 ÷ sin 35° ≈ 34.9 m), not the horizontal distance: ask 'Which side does the question ask for?'
records.reference: KICD Grade 10 Mathematics, 2.4 Trigonometry 1; OpenStax, Algebra and Trigonometry, right-triangle trigonometry (SOH-CAH-TOA)

records.why: Two fixes in one edit. (1) Problem 2 said 'horizontal span of the roof is 10 m'. 'Span' normally means the full width of the roof, which is not the run to the ridge, and 10 m at 30° gives a ridge 5.8 m above the wall, too tall for a maize store. It now says what is measured (6 m, ridge height 6 tan 30° = 3.46 m). (2) Expected answers for all four problems were missing; added and checked: 8 sin 15° = 2.07 m; 6 tan 30° = 3.46 m; 32 tan 62° = 32 x 1.8807 = 60.18 m; tan⁻¹(1/3) = 18.43°.
records.old: Find the vertical height the ramp rises. Problem 2 — A maize store in Eldoret has a sloped roof. The roof rises at 30° (a special angle). The horizontal span of the roof is 10 m. Find the height of the roof above the horizontal span. Problem 3 — A surveyor in Garissa measures that a telecom tower casts a shadow 32 m long when the sun's angle of elevation is 62°. Find the height of the tower. Problem 4 — A road in the Kericho tea plantation rises 18 m vertically over a horizontal distance of 54 m. Find the angle of inclination of the road (use inverse tangent).
records.new: Find the vertical height the ramp rises. (Answer: 8 × sin 15° ≈ 8 × 0.2588 ≈ 2.07 m.) Problem 2 — A maize store in Eldoret has a sloped roof. The roof rises at 30° (a special angle). The horizontal distance from the wall to the point directly below the ridge is 6 m. Find the height of the ridge above the wall. (Answer: 6 × tan 30° = 2√3 ≈ 3.46 m.) Problem 3 — A surveyor in Garissa measures that a telecom tower casts a shadow 32 m long when the sun's angle of elevation is 62°. Find the height of the tower. (Answer: 32 × tan 62° ≈ 32 × 1.881 ≈ 60.2 m.) Problem 4 — A road in the Kericho tea plantation rises 18 m vertically over a horizontal distance of 54 m. Find the angle of inclination of the road (use inverse tangent). (Answer: tan⁻¹(18/54) ≈ 18.4°.)

records.why: A 12° slope is far too steep for a wheelchair ramp. Common accessibility guidance uses a gradient of about 1 in 12, which is only about 4.8° (tan⁻¹(1/12) = 4.76°; for example the US ADA Standards, section 405). Teaching a 12° 'wheelchair ramp' is the wrong safety message for the PCI of safety and for a hospital. The numbers and answers (6.13 m) are unchanged; only the purpose of the ramp is changed.

records.why: Problem 3 (the dhow, 27 m cliff, 41°) can only be solved if learners know that the angle of depression equals the angle at the boat. The lesson only mentioned this 'alternate angles' idea at the very end, in the Model Building phase, after the problem set, and the demonstration did not show it. Added the step where it is first needed (guideline 4) and the common mistake to watch for (guideline 5). Check: 20 / tan 35° = 20 / 0.7002 = 28.6 m, matching the existing demonstration.

records.new: For the Fort Jesus demonstration, draw the horizontal line at the cliff top and mark the 35° angle of depression DOWNWARD from it. Then draw the ground line from the foot of the cliff to the dhow and show that the same 35° angle appears inside the triangle at the dhow (alternate angles between the two horizontal lines). Say: 'The angle of depression at the top equals the angle of elevation at the dhow. So the cliff, 20 m, is OPPOSITE the 35° angle, and the distance d is ADJACENT: tan 35° = 20 ÷ d.' If a learner writes the 35° inside the triangle at the top, ask: 'From which line is an angle of depression measured, the horizontal or the cliff?' Teacher ends Part B by pointing to the prediction board:

records.why: Fort Jesus is described as a cliff 20 m, 27 m and (in the unit text) 30 m high. The fort stands on a low coral ridge and its sea-facing walls are lower than that, and the three heights do not agree. This needs local knowledge, so it is flagged rather than guessed: either use a real, measured height, or describe the place as 'a coastal cliff near Mombasa' and keep the numbers.

records.why: The rubric used only the internal names (excellent, proficient, developing). Each descriptor now starts with the CBE level name (Exceeds, Meets, Approaches Expectations) so teachers and learners see the CBE level the descriptor describes. The descriptor wording is unchanged.

value.criterion: Labelling and choosing the correct ratio
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Draws accurate, fully labelled triangles with opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse correct relative to the given angle, and justifies every ratio choice using SOH-CAH-TOA.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Labels triangles mostly correctly and chooses the right ratio, but the justification is brief or incomplete.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Labels sides incorrectly or does not give a reason for choosing the ratio.

value.criterion: Calculation and use of tables, calculator or exact values
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Sets up and rearranges equations correctly, calculates accurately (mast about 47.7 m, ramp about 6.13 m, exact special-angle values) with units and sensible rounding.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Sets up equations correctly with minor arithmetic, rounding or unit errors.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Equations are set up incorrectly or the calculation is mostly incorrect or incomplete.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Clearly explains sin θ = cos(90° − θ) using opposite/adjacent swapping and proves tan θ = sin θ ÷ cos θ from the definitions.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: States the relationships correctly but explanation or proof is partial.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: States the relationships without explanation or with errors.

value.criterion: Elevation, depression and connection to the phenomenon
value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Correctly distinguishes elevation from depression, explains why they are equal, and clearly links all work to how the Nakuru mast height is found without climbing.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Defines elevation and depression correctly with a weak link to the phenomenon.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Confuses elevation and depression or does not connect the work to the mast.

value.excellent: Exceeds Expectations: Gives a clear general method and relevant Kenyan examples, with well-organised working and full-sentence conclusions.
value.proficient: Meets Expectations: Gives a reasonable method and examples, with some gaps in organisation.
value.developing: Approaches Expectations: Gives little or unclear reference to real-life use and working is disorganised.

records.why: CBE has four levels: Exceeds, Meets, Approaches and Below Expectations. The data contract allows only three level fields per criterion (excellent, proficient, developing) and the printed headings are fixed by the template, so the Below Expectations level cannot be represented. Teachers could add it by hand (for example 'work not yet showing the Approaches descriptor') until the contract allows four levels.
